metaDescription: Five 5 channel streaming mixers compared on USB recording, phantom power, Bluetooth and EQ, so a small desk can mix mic, music and game audio.
expertTake: The Aveek 5 Channel is the best streaming mixer in this group because it ties a built in PC recording interface to 48V phantom power and USB playback on a compact board. The BOMGE 5 Channel is the value pick for a streamer who likes hands on echo and delay. Anyone who needs two or more XLR microphones should step up to a mixer with a published preamp count.
introParagraphs: Five channels is a sweet spot for a small streaming desk: one microphone, a music source, a phone, a second line input and a spare. It is large enough to feel like a real mixer and small enough to fit beside a keyboard.

The catch is that a five channel label describes inputs, not microphone preamps, and most boards in this size class carry a single XLR channel. The questions that matter are whether the unit talks to a computer over USB, whether it powers a condenser microphone, and how it handles the other channels.

products.name: Aveek 5 channel mixer with PC recording interface
products.description:
Aveek's five channel board is the most complete package in this size class on paper. It carries a built in recording interface so a PC sees it as a sound card, 48V phantom power for condenser microphones, Bluetooth for a phone and USB playback for music beds. That covers the usual streaming checklist without extra adapters.

What keeps it from being a studio console is its price tier and its simplicity. The preamp is a single channel affair, effects are a bonus rather than a selling point, and there is no standalone recording. Compared with the Socodox it focuses on connectivity rather than a larger effects library, which makes it easier to learn and quicker to set up for a first stream.

Ownership is mostly about discipline. Set gain so peaks stay out of the red, use balanced cables to keep hiss down and give the board its own USB port. Keep a small supply of spare cables, because a mixer with this many connection types gets plugged and unplugged often and the ports see wear. Label each cable at both ends so a rushed swap before going live does not send the music into the microphone channel. If the board has a ground lift or noise switch, learn what it does before the day you need it.
products.bestFor: A single streamer who wants USB recording, phantom power and music playback on one small board.
pros: USB playback for music and bumpers
cons: Single mic channel limits it to one voice

products.name: Socodox 5 channel mixer with 99 DSP effects
products.description:
The Socodox leans on tone shaping: a three band EQ, 99 DSP effects, 48V phantom power, Bluetooth and USB recording. For a streamer who enjoys shaping a voice with a few knobs rather than software plug ins, it offers more surface control than the plainer boards.

The tradeoff is that a long effect list is not the same as a better microphone path. The preamp is a single stage, and reverb on a voice is often more distracting than helpful in a stream. Beside the BOMGE it has a more conventional EQ section, while the BOMGE leans on echo and delay.

Over time you will probably use the EQ and the phantom switch daily and the effects rarely. Save a preset knob position with tape marks or a photo, keep the USB cable short and avoid running the board near a router or power brick that adds interference.
products.bestFor: Streamers who like to shape their voice with onboard EQ and a few effects.
pros: Three band EQ for voice shaping

products.name: BOMGE 5 channel digital mixer with echo and delay
products.description:
BOMGE's five channel sound board mixes USB, Bluetooth, echo and delay effects and 48V phantom power in a digital package. The interface is aimed at casual streamers and karaoke style use, where a quick echo on a voice is part of the fun.

It stays modest in aim. There is no published preamp gain figure, so treat quiet dynamic microphones carefully, and expect the effects to matter more than the preamp. Next to the Aveek it trades some polish for echo controls, but it still handles the basic job of getting a microphone and a phone into a PC.

If you pair it with a sensitive condenser mic, set the gain conservatively and watch for hiss at the noise floor. A small pop filter and a boom arm usually improve the recorded voice more than any change inside the box. Since the effects here are aimed at fun rather than polish, treat echo as a seasoning for a specific segment and bypass it for ordinary talk, because a constant tail on every word tires listeners quickly.
products.bestFor: Casual streamers who want echo and delay effects on a compact USB board.
pros: Echo and delay effects built in
cons: No published gain figure for dynamic mics
Digital effects suit casual use more than serious streams

products.name: Mackie Mix5 5 channel compact analog mixer
products.description:
The Mackie Mix5 is the outlier here: a straightforward analog compact mixer with no USB, no Bluetooth and no effects. Its job is to blend a microphone and line sources with a plain signal path, and then hand the result to a separate audio interface, capture card or the computer's line input.

That makes it unusual for streaming, but useful for someone who already owns an interface. The tactile knobs and fixed layout never change, and there is no software to update. The cost is that you need another box to connect to the PC, so the combined desk space and cabling can exceed a USB board such as the Aveek.

Ownership is low drama. Analog mixers age gracefully, controls can be cleaned with contact cleaner, and nothing becomes obsolete when an operating system updates. Plan on a quality cable between the mixer and the interface, and keep the output level moderate to avoid overloading the interface input. A common setup is to send the main mix to the interface and use the headphone output for monitoring, with the master fader parked near its marked unity position. Dust covers are cheap insurance on a board that sits open on a desk for years.
products.bestFor: Streamers who already have an interface and want a plain analog mix stage.
pros: No software or drivers to maintain
Works with any interface or capture device
cons: No USB connection of its own

products.name: TAVOSOP 5 channel mixer with 99 DSP, USB, OTG and LED lights
products.description:
TAVOSOP adds OTG support and LED lighting to a five channel console with 99 DSP effects. OTG means a phone can serve as the host, which suits a mobile streamer working from a handset rather than a PC.

The lighting and effects are cosmetic, but the OTG feature is practical for a creator who streams from a phone. Compared with the Socodox, it focuses on mobile compatibility, while the Socodox focuses on EQ. Check the listing details for phantom power and preamp specifics before buying, since the title does not spell them out.

Keep expectations realistic about gain and noise. A phone USB port supplies limited power, so use a powered setup when possible and check that the phone supports the mixer in class compliant mode. Before buying, read recent owner feedback for your phone model, because Android handling of external USB audio varies between makers and system versions, and an adapter that works on one handset can fail on another.
products.bestFor: Mobile streamers who connect through a phone with OTG.
pros: LED lighting for a desk look
Five channels on a compact board
cons: Key preamp specs are thin in the listing

buyingCriteria.explanation: A five channel board such as the Aveek, Socodox or BOMGE usually has one XLR microphone preamp, with the other channels used for line and stereo sources. If you plan a co host, check that two XLR inputs exist, because a five channel label alone does not promise them. A useful workaround for a second voice is a small USB microphone on a separate computer input, though that route skips the mixer's EQ and gain controls and makes level matching harder. For a solo stream, one real preamp is plenty.

A mixer with a built in interface presents itself to the PC as a sound card. The Aveek, Socodox and BOMGE list USB connection, while the Mackie Mix5 does not and needs a separate interface. Skipping that step saves a box and a cable run. It also removes a place where noise can creep in, since an analog hand off between two devices is another opportunity for a ground loop. If you go the Mix5 route, a balanced connection into the interface and a short cable keep that hand off clean.
Condenser microphones need 48V. The Aveek, Socodox and BOMGE list it. The Mackie Mix5 is an analog mixer, so confirm phantom support in its manual before pairing it with a condenser.

A three band EQ like the Socodox's shapes a voice far more usefully than 99 reverbs. For speech, cutting low frequency rumble and a touch of presence beats echo, so prioritize the EQ section. A practical recipe is to roll off the lowest band slightly to tame desk thumps and breath rumble, add a small lift in the upper mids for clarity and leave the effects off during talking segments. Test the settings on a recording of your own voice before going live, because a headset reads differently from a studio microphone.

Bluetooth and OTG help creators who stream from a handset. The TAVOSOP adds OTG while the Aveek and BOMGE offer Bluetooth. A phone USB port supplies limited power, so powered operation is safer. Streaming from a handset also adds heat and battery drain, so a charger or a powered hub in the chain avoids the phone shutting down halfway through a long session. Keep the phone's notifications off so alerts never mix into the broadcast.

USB playback lets you trigger an intro or music bed without a computer. The Aveek lists it, which is handy for solo streamers who do not want to alt tab to a music player. Keep the music well below the voice, around fifteen to twenty decibels under speech, and avoid commercial tracks that can trigger copyright claims on a live platform. Royalty free libraries load cleanly onto a USB drive and play through the playback input without touching the computer's mixer.

howWeEvaluated.title: Connection range
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at USB, Bluetooth, OTG and playback options on each unit, because a streaming mixer lives or dies by how many sources it can take without adapters. The Aveek leads with PC recording and USB playback, while the TAVOSOP adds OTG for phones. The Mackie Mix5 scored lower here by design, since it has no digital connection at all.

howWeEvaluated.title: Microphone path
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked for phantom power and the number of XLR inputs, noting that gain figures are not published for most boards here. Where a listing was silent we treated the preamp as basic and recommended a forgiving microphone, rather than assuming performance that the spec sheet does not support. A published figure counts for more than a flattering adjective.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tone control
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed EQ depth against effects count. The Socodox's three band EQ rated higher than extra reverbs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Simplicity
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how fast a first stream can start. The Mackie Mix5 is plain but needs an interface, while the Aveek is close to plug and play. We also looked at how many knobs a streamer must touch to change a level, and whether the labels are readable in a dim room, since stream desks are rarely well lit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared price tiers, with the Mackie Mix5 and Aveek at the mid and lower end and the TAVOSOP in the middle.

faq.q: Do five channels mean five microphones?
faq.a: No. Most five channel boards have one XLR mic input and use the rest for line and stereo sources. Check the listing before planning a co host.

faq.q: Which is best for a first stream?
faq.a: The Aveek 5 Channel is the easiest, with PC recording, phantom power and USB playback. It needs little setup, so a new streamer can plug in a microphone, pick the board as the recording device in the streaming software and be live within a short session. Spend the saved effort on room treatment and microphone placement, which improve the sound far more than any switch on the board.

faq.q: Do I need an audio interface with these?
faq.a: Not with the Aveek, Socodox or BOMGE, which include USB connection. The Mackie Mix5 does need one.

Rarely for speech. EQ and compression matter more, and a voice buried in reverb is harder to understand on a phone speaker. Use effects sparingly, for a single segment or a joke, and leave them off for the main talking portions of a stream.

faq.q: Can I stream from a phone with these?
faq.a: The TAVOSOP lists OTG for phones. Others may work via Bluetooth, but check your phone's compatibility, because Bluetooth adds delay that makes live monitoring awkward. For a handset stream, a wired OTG connection is steadier and usually carries better audio than a wireless link, provided the phone supplies enough power to the mixer.

faq.q: How much gain do I need?
faq.a: Dynamic mics need around 60 to 70 dB. Most boards here do not publish gain, so use a condenser or an inline booster if levels are low. An inline booster adds a clean stage of gain between the microphone and the mixer, which is cheaper than replacing the board. Raising gain in software afterward lifts the noise floor along with the voice, so fix level at the source first.
